Definition — FEMA: the Foreign Exchange Management Act — the law governing what non-residents may hold in India and how money crosses the border. Its property rules now live in the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019. How the source of funds decides repatriation The question nobody asks until selling: where did the purchase money COME from? NRE/FCNR (foreign currency) funding: full repatriation of proceeds — but only for two residential properties in a lifetime without special approval. NRO funding or Indian income: repatriation capped at USD 1 million per financial year, whatever the property count. Bought while still a resident: the same 1-million-per-year route through an NRO account. The account choice at purchase becomes irreversible history at sale. Repatriating inherited property Allowed — within the same framework: documentary proof of inheritance, taxes settled, the annual limit observed. The paperwork order matters more than the principle. Even after a legitimate sale, repatriation follows the standard annual framework. Inherit-only, sell-to-residents-only, repatriate-within-caps: that layered fence is where NRI families stumble years later. How repatriation actually works, step by step 1. Sale proceeds land in an NRO account — the mandatory starting point. 2. File the income-tax return for the sale year. 3. A chartered accountant issues Form 15CB confirming capital-gains tax is paid. 4. Submit Form 15CA online with the sale deed and bank statements. 5. The bank verifies, converts, remits. Not one bank visit — a CA, a bank and the tax department all signing off; budget weeks, not days. Red flags Cash, or any channel outside normal banking — an outright FEMA violation; every rupee must move through banks. Skipped or botched 15CA/15CB filings — transfers block. Like citizen Aadhaar, the point is one verifiable identity that stays consistent across every department, bank and registration office. The problem it solves India has over 600 million parcels, and historically each state tracked them its own way — survey numbers, khasra numbers, patta numbers, tax accounts — none linked automatically. The same land wearing four numbers in four registers is exactly the confusion fraudsters exploited: multi-selling the same plot under its different identities. How far the rollout has reached Uneven, and that unevenness decides its usefulness for YOUR parcel. Andhra Pradesh finished first at full coverage (60+ million parcels); Karnataka, Odisha, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh sit in the 60–90% band; some large states lag far behind. Nationally, roughly half of parcels carry a ULPIN. No ULPIN on your parcel = none of the benefits yet — the traditional checks carry the full weight. It cannot verify the seller’s title, and cannot reach back into unregistered history. And within even high-coverage states, parcels miss IDs where surveys are incomplete or boundaries disputed. Treat it as a checksum on identity that narrows your work — the title chain, EC and litigation checks remain the work itself. Market value for land runs on registered comparables, frontage, road access and zone. The two numbers, defined Guideline value (circle rate, ready-reckoner rate, unit rate — the name varies by state): the registration department’s benchmark valuation for each locality and land type, existing to stop parties under-declaring prices to dodge duty. The Income Tax Act sweeps all the local names into one term: the stamp duty value . Market value : what a willing buyer actually pays a willing seller — set by demand, not by notification. Duty runs on the higher number Duty is computed on the guideline value or the declared price, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. Declaring a lower price does not help — where the declared figure falls below the benchmark, the department simply applies the benchmark. Exact rates vary by state; calculate with your jurisdiction’s numbers. The trap: buying below the guideline value Buying ABOVE the benchmark costs you duty; buying BELOW it can cost you INCOME TAX. Under Section 56(2)(x), where you buy immovable property for less than its stamp-duty value, the shortfall is treated as YOUR income under “Income from Other Sources” (subject to the tolerance band). A genuine bargain thus gets taxed as if the discount were a gift to you. One protective mechanism: where agreement and registration dates differ, the benchmark ON THE AGREEMENT DATE can be adopted — but only if part of the consideration moved by cheque, draft or electronic transfer on or before that date. A CASH token does not qualify. And states revise values periodically, so always verify the figure on the date that matters to YOUR transaction. Example: You agree a plot at ₹60 lakh in March by handshake; the state revises the guideline to ₹75 lakh in April; you register in June. Duty computes on ₹75 lakh — and 56(2)(x) can tax ₹15 lakh as your income. Had you paid even a ₹1 lakh token by BANK TRANSFER with a written agreement in March, the March benchmark could have locked. The transfer mode of one token payment carried lakhs of consequence. What moves the guideline value Location does most of the work — established and fast-developing pockets carry higher benchmarks because demand is already on record. Then: zoning — what the land may legally be used for feeds the assessed band; infrastructure — a new road or transit line lifts the benchmark, but only at the NEXT revision; and revision frequency itself varies by state, which is why benchmarks drift from reality in both directions. What determines market value For land the drivers are physical and legal, not cosmetic: frontage and road width; corner position; whether the survey number matches the ground; the master-plan zone and whether conversion is complete; and above all, what comparable parcels nearby actually REGISTERED for — a different number from what they were advertised at. Duty on the benchmark anyway — plus possible 56(2)(x) income in your hands. Is guideline always lower than market? Market value — built from registered comparables; the guideline only tells you the state’s floor. Approval depends on the master plan, zoning and state land-use law — not on willingness to pay. Green belts, protected agricultural zones, forests and environmentally restricted land often cannot be converted at any price. The order comes from the competent planning or revenue authority, with documents and a site inspection. Buying land “already converted”? Verify the order is VALID and unexpired — a lapsed conversion reverts the land to agricultural. Agricultural vs residential land: the real difference Agricultural land is meant for farming, and its registration, taxation and transfer rules all follow from that purpose. Converted land costs more per square yard — but it carries the legal standing you need to build, raise a home loan, or sell to someone who will. The premium is not decoration; it is the difference between a plot and a field. What the law actually requires Start with the MASTER PLAN, not the application form — this is where most people get the sequence backwards. Formal conversion approval from the competent planning or revenue authority is required before agricultural land can legally host residential construction, and that approval must align with the master plan zone, the zoning classification, and the state’s land-revenue statutes. Two hard truths follow: where the plan already designates the land residential, conversion is not discretionary — it should be granted; where the plan marks the zone green belt, forest or agriculture-protection, conversion is simply NOT AVAILABLE. No fee fixes a blocking zone. Definition — Master plan: the government’s long-term land-use map for a region — which areas are residential, commercial, industrial, green. In conversion matters it outranks everything: the plan decides what is possible; the application only executes it. Documents you will need ☐ Title deed and the 30-year chain of title. ☐ Updated land-record extract — registered deed, 7/12, patta, or your state’s equivalent (pattadar passbook in Telangana). ☐ Survey sketch, master plan extract, and an EC. ☐ NOCs from agriculture, town planning, forest or water-resources departments where applicable. Getting the file right the FIRST time saves months of back-and-forth. The step-by-step process 1) Pull the master plan extract; confirm the zone permits residential use. 2) File the application with the revenue or planning authority for your state and zone. 3) Pay the conversion fee — assessed on area, location and proposed use. 4) Site inspection: an official verifies the land matches the application. 5) Receive the conversion order; the land record is updated. 6) READ THE CONDITIONS on pages two and three — they decide whether the order stays alive. 7) Apply for building-plan sanction from the local body before any construction starts — conversion permits the USE; the sanction permits the BUILDING. Common challenges The zone itself blocking the change — no application can convert green-belt, forest or protection-zone land. Delays or rejection from incomplete files, missing NOCs, or mismatches found at inspection. And the quiet one: conversion orders that LAPSE because construction timelines or conditions went unmet — leaving the land agricultural despite a framed approval on the wall. Example: A buyer pays a premium for a “converted” plot with a 2019 order. Condition 4 on page two required construction to commence within three years; nothing was built. The order lapsed in 2022 — the parcel is agricultural again, and the premium bought paper. One reading of the conditions would have repriced the deal. Best practices before you start Master plan zone first; then road access, water and soil. A short consultation with a local surveyor costs less than discovering a blocking issue after the fee is paid. And engage someone who knows THAT district’s revenue office — procedures genuinely differ between neighbouring districts. Quick answers (FAQ) Is conversion mandatory before building a house? Generally yes — building on unconverted agricultural land invites demolition and denies you sanction, loans and clean resale. Who approves? The competent revenue or planning authority (RDO/Collector-side in Telangana, with HMDA/DTCP layers for layouts). Can any land be converted if I pay? No — the zone decides; money cannot move a green belt. Does an order expire? Yes — it is conditional and time-bound; verify validity when buying “converted” land. Can NRIs apply? For land they lawfully hold (e.g. inherited) — subject to the same zoning rules. If I skip conversion? Unauthorised use: penalties, demolition risk, no sanction, and a discount when you sell. Bottom line Conversion is a sequence, not a fee: zone first, statute second, payment last — and the order you receive is a living document with conditions and an expiry. Read it like a contract, because it is one. For you: This is the machinery of your margin: farmland in, NA/DTCP-approved plots out. Your edge is the SEQUENCE discipline — verify the master-plan zone before the land is even priced, and when buying “converted” parcels from others, audit the order’s conditions and dates like a bank would. 2026-11-21|ls-agri-loans: Bank loans for agricultural land: eligibility, documents, and how to apply Land School · source: “Bank Loans for Agricultural Land: Eligibility, Documents, and How to Apply” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Agricultural land loans are regulated, secured credit under priority-sector lending — not moneylender territory. Farmers, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, SHG members and women applicants all have defined qualifying paths. Banks typically fund 70–85% of valuation at roughly 7–12% a year; tenures can stretch to 15 years. What the bank checks is your land record: deed, RoR, mutation, survey match, valuation, classification. Under interest subvention, prompt repayers on eligible loans can reach an effective ~4%. You do NOT need to already own land — a registered sale agreement on a clean-title plot gets the file moving. What this loan is Secured credit for buying, developing or cultivating farmland, offered under India’s priority-sector framework by public banks, private lenders, NBFCs and regional rural banks. The distinction worth stating plainly: a land purchase loan is a one-time TERM loan secured on the land; a Kisan Credit Card is revolving working capital for crop seasons. Both are “agricultural credit”, which is why they get conflated — but no bank sanctions a land purchase against a KCC limit. Coverage extends to developing fallow land, horticulture and dairying moves, and irrigation or soil improvement on land already owned. What the bank actually verifies Borrower’s capacity — farm records, bank statements or ITRs. Seller’s title — sale deed, Record of Rights, mutation and revenue records. Encumbrances that would block a fresh mortgage. Survey number and boundary matching the paper. An approved valuer’s price. And classification still AGRICULTURAL — reclassified land needs a different product entirely. Definition — Record of Rights (RoR): the state’s core revenue record of who holds each parcel — pattadar passbook in Telangana, 7/12 in Maharashtra, patta in Tamil Nadu. Every bank wants the latest one, whatever the local name. Who can apply RBI priority-sector norms shape it: applicants ~18–65 at maturity; active farmers the default category (a credible farm business plan can work with some lenders); marginal farmers (up to a hectare) often prioritised, small farmers (1–2 ha) eligible; tenant farmers, sharecroppers and landless labourers enter through self-help or joint-liability groups where collective liability replaces collateral; women qualify on equal terms, with several public banks prioritising distress applicants and widows. And you need not own land already — a registered sale agreement on the target plot, with clean seller title, starts the process. Documents you will need Identity (Aadhaar/PAN/Voter ID); address proof; the land file — sale deed, revenue record, survey report; the registered sale agreement; and repayment evidence — bank statements or ITRs. Above ₹3 lakh, add a valuer’s report and legal clearance certificate. The universal requirement under many names: the latest RoR plus updated mutation entries. How the application runs Compare a few nearby lenders → assemble the file BEFORE the branch visit → apply (often online) → the bank verifies documents, inspects the land, orders valuation — larger loans get a legal title search → sanction letter → funds on creation of the mortgage. With clean paper, public banks finish in three to six weeks; unclear land records are the number-one stall. Pitfalls and red flags Survey number not matching ground boundaries — the most common holdup; land quietly reclassified non-agricultural — rules out the product; an undisclosed encumbrance surfacing in the legal search — weeks lost; an UNregistered sale agreement — dead end at most lenders; and chain gaps — the slowest of all to clear. Example: Use the bank as your unpaid second lawyer: even buying with your own cash, run the parcel through a lender’s eyes. A sanction is a quality certificate; a refusal names the defect the seller did not. Rates, amounts, repayment 70–85% of valuation funded; 7–12% yearly by lender and size; tenure to 15 years (7–10 typical); repayment often aligned to harvest cycles rather than flat EMIs; minimal prepayment charges on floating rates; processing fees commonly waived below ₹3 lakh. Government schemes that cut the cost KCC — subsidised revolving credit, useful working capital alongside an acquisition. Modified Interest Subvention — up to ₹3 lakh at a concessional 7%, with a 3% prompt-repayment incentive taking the effective rate to ~4%. RKVY — state-channelled land-development funding. PM Fasal Bima — crop insurance tied to loans, protecting repayment when a season fails. The direction of policy is expansion: agricultural credit targets keep rising year on year. Pre-application checklist ☐ Classification confirmed agricultural in current records. ☐ Survey number and boundaries matching deed AND ground. ☐ Encumbrances, liens, litigation searched. ☐ Sale agreement REGISTERED before it goes to the bank. ☐ 6–12 months of statements / income records assembled. ☐ Subvention eligibility checked before signing. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a first-time farmer get a purchase loan? Yes — eligibility paths exist without prior ownership; the plan and the plot’s paper carry the file. How much will the bank fund? 70–85% of ITS valuation — usually conservative against your negotiated price; budget the gap. What if the survey number mismatches the ground? Fix it before applying; it will stall everything else anyway. Bottom line The loan is accessible and, with schemes, cheaper than it looks. Speed is decided upstream — by the state of the land’s paperwork before the application. Title, survey and encumbrance sorted early turn a three-month file into a three-week one. For you: Financeability is a quality grade on the LAND, not just the borrower — it widens your exit, because your future buyer probably needs the loan even if you never did. Unfinanceable land trades at a structural discount at BOTH ends; price that honestly. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). Ceiling laws cap the total holding — and the cap moves by state and land type. Verification means pulling deed, EC and revenue records YOURSELF — most disputes start in skipped paperwork. The negotiated price is the start of spending: duty, registration, legal and survey fees stack on top. NRIs cannot buy farmland outright — inheritance is their route in. Who can legally buy The land’s state decides, through its land-reform laws. Restricted states demand an agricultural background or eligibility test (with exemption and family routes for some non-farmers); open states — Telangana included — let anyone buy. On top sits the ceiling: a cap on total holdings that varies by state and land type, and crossing it can void the excess. Confirm both BEFORE attachment to a plot sets in. What verification covers, and why The step that decides whether the purchase becomes an asset or a decade of correspondence. The core: title deed — name matches the seller; EC for 15–30 years — loans and claims; latest revenue records — ownership and classification cross-checked (pattadar passbook in Telangana); mutation — actually updated, because an unmutated transfer can be contested later; licensed survey — boundaries on the ground match the paper; encroachment is more common than first-timers expect. The agreement then fixes price, advance and timelines, with the seller’s identity proof and confirmation the land remains agricultural-classified. Example: The skipped-survey classic: 4 acres bought on paper, 3.7 on the ground — the missing 0.3 under a neighbour’s decades-old bund. The survey that would have caught it costs a few thousand rupees; the shortfall cost lakhs and a boundary case. The process in order Eligibility → verification file → agreement (price, advance, timelines) → registered deed at the SRO with duty and fees → mutation so the record names you. Each step gates the next; hurrying the order is how buyers finance other people’s mistakes. The real total cost Beyond the price: stamp duty and registration (state-set — in Telangana around 7.5% all-in on sale deeds), surveyor’s fees, legal consultation, EC charges — several percentage points above the negotiated figure. Planning to build later? Conversion is a separate application, inspection and state-specific fee again. Red flags Ownership disputes and fraud tied to murky chains; government-allotted / assigned land that cannot legally be resold — including land granted to SC/ST families under protective laws, whose restrictions surface only after payment; unchecked mutation; unsurveyed boundaries. The first two are WALK-AWAY flags; the last two are FIX-FIRST flags. Restricted states vs open states Aspect Agriculturist-restricted states Open-purchase states Who may buy Farming background / eligibility tests required Any buyer Legal source State land-reform law State land-reform law Extra friction Exemption applications, proof of background None on eligibility (ceiling still applies) Suits Active farmers Investors and non-farming buyers NRI restrictions A hard line: NRIs and OCIs cannot purchase agricultural land directly under the exchange-control rules; they CAN inherit it. RBI approval exists in theory, rarely in practice, and leans toward genuine agricultural use. (The full NRI story — funding accounts, repatriation caps — is its own class in this school.) Financing reality Banks lend against farmland more cautiously than against houses — expect more cash upfront, slower sanctions, and a lender re-running your whole verification. Use that: a bank’s refusal is free due diligence naming the defect. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Eligibility confirmed for the state. ☐ EC and title deed pulled by YOU. ☐ Latest revenue records compared against the deed for name/classification mismatches. ☐ Mutation status verified. ☐ Licensed survey done before the agreement. ☐ Assigned/restricted-origin ruled out. ☐ Full friction cost (duty + fees) priced into the offer. Quick answers (FAQ) Can anyone buy, or only farmers? Depends on the state — Telangana: anyone; several states: restrictions apply. How far back should the history check go? 30 years standard. Can the land be converted later? If zoning allows — a separate process with its own fee. What are the total costs? Price + roughly 7.5% duty/registration (Telangana) + legal, survey and EC costs. Bottom line Agricultural land rewards patience over speed: eligibility, ceiling, chain, record-match, survey — five checks before money, each cheap, each catching a different disaster. The dispute you avoid was always cheaper than the discount you chased. For you: Make the ritual fixed and identical per parcel: portal check → passbook-vs-deed match → EC 30 years → prohibited-list → chain → survey → THEN price. Ritual beats judgement; it has no optimistic days. And each defect found is either a WALK (assigned taint, water-body extent) or a PRICE (pending mutation, survey shortfall) — knowing which bucket instantly is what “experienced” means. 2026-11-23|ls-scams: Common land scams in India and how to protect yourself Land School · source: “Common Land Scams in India and How to Protect Yourself” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. 2026-11-23|ls-patta-vs-deed: The real difference between patta, sale deed, and title deed Land School · source: “The Real Difference Between Patta, Sale Deed, and Title Deed” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Patta vs sale deed = tax record vs transfer of ownership. Only one moves title. A patta SUPPORTS an ownership claim; it does not create one — no court treats it as proof of title. “Title deed” is not a document at all — it is the category term for the registered instruments behind your ownership chain. When patta and deed disagree, the registered deed generally prevails — but the mismatch still blocks resale and loans until mutation fixes it. Revenue records wear different names across states; the administrative job is the same. Why the difference matters Three documents, three different questions. A patta answers: whose name does the revenue department hold against this survey number? A sale deed answers: did a legal transfer occur? A title deed answers: is the ownership chain behind that transfer clean? Confusing them is not a vocabulary slip — it decides which paper a buyer trusts when the papers conflict. What a patta records — and does not Issued by the revenue department, not a court: landholder’s name, extent, survey number. Its function is administrative — tax assessment and revenue tracking. Real uses: banks ask for it before lending against land; it supports a possession claim in a dispute; it confirms the parcel exists in state records under a stated name. What it does NOT do is create ownership — courts have consistently held revenue records are evidence of possession, not conclusive proof of title. (Telangana’s pattadar passbook, Maharashtra’s 7/12, Karnataka’s RTC — different names, same administrative job.) Why the registered sale deed carries the most weight The deed is the instrument that MOVES ownership; registration is what gives it force. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act: any sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires a registered instrument — which, at that threshold, means EVERY land sale in India; the folk belief that registration only applies above some higher value is simply wrong. Section 17 of the Registration Act makes the registration compulsory; and Section 49 delivers the consequence — an unregistered document that required registration cannot even be received as evidence of the transaction. Registration also feeds the public record every future EC draws from: the paper trail exists because the statute compels it. “Title deed” is a category, not a certificate No office in India issues a document titled “title deed”. The term describes whichever registered instruments TOGETHER establish you hold the property free of competing claims: your registered sale deed plus the deeds behind it — earlier sales, partitions, gifts — back to the Mother Deed that first established ownership. When a bank asks for “title documents”, it wants that SET. And a title deed’s strength is borrowed: exactly as strong as the registered instruments standing behind it, and no stronger. Definition — Mother Deed: the earliest traceable document that established ownership of the parcel — the root of the chain. Every later deed inherits its validity from this root; a defect there flows down through everything. The three compared Aspect Patta / revenue record Sale deed Title deed Issued by Revenue department Executed by parties, registered at SRO Not issued — the chain of registered instruments Function Tax + revenue tracking Transfers ownership Establishes the clean chain Legal weight Evidence of possession The operative instrument As strong as the deeds composing it Buyer’s use Cross-check + loan requirement The document you actually acquire by What your advocate traces 30 years back When patta and deed disagree The registered deed generally prevails — ownership does not wait for the revenue record to catch up. But the mismatch still does practical damage: a patta in the previous owner’s name stalls your RESALE (the next buyer’s advocate flags it), stalls a LOAN (the bank matches patta name against deed), and can send tax demands to the wrong person for years. The correction is MUTATION: file with the revenue authority, attaching the registered deed, EC, identity proof and the previous revenue record. Fix it because it blocks your next transaction — not because your ownership depends on it. Example: A buyer holds a clean 2021 registered deed but never mutated; the passbook still names the seller. In 2025 the resale buyer’s bank refuses sanction on the name mismatch, and the deal waits months for a mutation that would have taken weeks back in 2021. The deed was always enough for OWNERSHIP — never enough for the next transaction. Your document checklist ☐ Start with the registered sale deed — the heaviest of the three. ☐ Trace the chain behind it to the Mother Deed, watching for gaps. ☐ Compare patta vs deed on name, extent, survey number. ☐ File mutation if the revenue record lags. ☐ Pull a separate EC for hidden loans and claims. Quick answers (FAQ) Does a patta prove ownership? No — it supports possession; the registered deed chain proves title. Is a title deed the same as a sale deed? The sale deed is usually its main component; the title deed is the whole chain. Can I sell if the patta still shows the previous owner? Legally the deed lets you — practically, mutate first or watch buyers walk. Can an EC replace a patta? No — they answer different questions (registered transactions vs revenue holding); a full check uses both. Bottom line Deed for ownership, patta for the record, chain for confidence — verify all three and make them agree before money moves. Where they disagree, the deed wins the law and the mismatch loses you the deal. For you: Use the three-question frame in every negotiation: whose name does Dharani hold (patta)? did a registered transfer occur (deed)? is the chain clean to the root (title)? A seller strong on one and vague on the others has told you where to dig. And keep your own ventures’ trinity aligned — deed, passbook, mutation — plot by plot; it is what “clear-title developer” means in practice. What assigned patta actually is It reads like any other patta — survey number, name, extent, classification. Governments have allotted land to landless families, SC/ST beneficiaries, ex-servicemen and other eligible groups under welfare schemes — and the original assignment order carries the real terms: how long the beneficiary must hold, what the land may be used for, and whether government approval is needed before any sale. IPC 471 — USING a forged document as genuine — the section that can reach a buyer who registered a deed without ever checking its underlying conditions. This is the lesson’s hardest truth: in assigned-land cases the buyer is treated as a participant, not merely a victim. 2C patta ≠ assigned patta 2C patta : agricultural land formally CONVERTED for residential use — its one condition (agricultural classification) already resolved through a conversion order. No welfare distribution behind it, no community restriction, no lock-in on sale. Assigned patta : welfare redistribution, with conditions on who may own, how long they must hold, and whether it can be sold at all. The restriction does not expire — check buyer eligibility before going one step further. ☐ Even past the window, some schemes require written Collector permission before registration — confirm. ☐ Review the ownership history: a pattern of quick, repeated transfers is exactly what CB-CID investigations flag. 2026-11-24|ls-rfctlarr: Land acquisition by government: compensation rules under the RFCTLARR Act Land School · source: “Land Acquisition by Government: Compensation Rules Under RFCTLARR Act” by 1acre.in Key Highlights The RFCTLARR Act 2013 (in force 1 Jan 2014) replaced the colonial 1894 acquisition law. Compensation is a FORMULA: market value × rural/urban multiplier, then DOUBLED by a mandatory 100% solatium. Rural land multiplies 1.0–2.0 by distance from the urban centre (some states go higher); urban land sits at 1×. Crops, trees, wells, structures, severance damage and relocation costs are valued and ADDED. R&R benefits — housing, allowances, sometimes jobs or annuities — run alongside the cheque. An award that looks short can be formally challenged — and often is, successfully. What acquisition under RFCTLARR means The state’s power to compulsorily take private land for a public purpose against compensation fixed by law — fundamentally different from a voluntary sale. The 2013 Act was written to make the process humane, participative and transparent after 120 years of complaints about the 1894 law’s arbitrary payouts. It is the law behind every highway, ring road and industrial corridor — including the RRR’s. How compensation is calculated Step 1 — market value (Section 26): the Collector uses registered sale deeds of similar land from the prior three years, taking the HIGHEST of: the top comparable deed, the average of the top half of nearby deeds, or any consented negotiated amount. Step 2 — the multiplier: urban ×1; rural on a sliding 1.0–2.0 scale rising with distance from the urban centre — some states push rural factors higher still. Step 3 — solatium: 100% added on top, doubling the result. Step 4 — additions: structures, wells, trees, standing crops, severance and relocation. Definition — Solatium: a statutory 100% top-up recognising the sale was FORCED. On ₹50 lakh of assessed value it adds another ₹50 lakh — a real break from the 1894 law’s 30% cap. Definition — Severance: when a road takes a strip and leaves your remaining field cut off or oddly shaped, the damage to the REMAINDER is separately compensable — the head owners most often forget to claim. The multiplier bands at a glance Where the land sits Multiplier What that means with solatium Urban land 1.0× (some states allow more) ≈ 2× market value all-in Rural, near the urban centre 1.0–1.5× ≈ 2–3× market value Rural, far from the urban centre Up to 2.0× (higher in some states) ≈ 4× market value — and beyond where states enhance The 12% clock On top of everything, the Collector adds 12% per annum on market value, running from the Social Impact Assessment notification date until the award or possession — whichever comes first. A slow acquisition literally accrues interest for the owner; a mis-tracked SIA date silently underpays it. Rehabilitation and resettlement The Act’s Second Schedule adds a structured R&R package beyond cash: housing, transport and resettlement allowances, and in defined cases employment or annuity support — aimed at restoring livelihoods, not just replacing land value. Crucially it reaches beyond owners: agricultural labourers who worked the acquired fields can qualify without owning an inch. Consent rules for private and PPP projects Where private companies acquire for a public purpose: consent of at least 80% of affected families (70% for public-private partnerships), preceded by a Social Impact Assessment. Emergencies — disasters, critical defence — can invoke the fast-track and skip the SIA. Definition — Social Impact Assessment (SIA): the mandatory study of who is affected and how, done before ordinary acquisitions proceed. Its notification date also starts the 12% clock — a date worth recording the day it appears. Common mistakes in awards The urban multiplier applied to land that should be rural (understating badly); wells, trees and boundary structures skipped because they need a separate survey; the 12% amount miscalculated off the wrong SIA date; and livelihood-dependent families never told they qualify for R&R. None are exotic — all are line-checkable. How to challenge an award An undervalued award is not final because the Collector signed it: apply for a reference to the LARR Authority within the time limit, and appeal onward to the High Court if needed. Most successful challenges trace to exactly the mistakes above — wrong multiplier, missed assets, miscalculated solatium or interest. Check every line before accepting; enhancement is common enough to be a strategy. Example: A Shadnagar-belt farmer’s award used three-year-old registered deeds from a corridor where real prices had doubled — and applied a 1.2 multiplier where distance justified 1.8. Documented recent comparables plus the correct band, argued at reference, materially enhanced the award. The formula is fair; the INPUTS are where owners win or lose. Bottom line The framework is fair on paper; implementation slips are where money leaks — a wrong multiplier here, a missed well there, an SIA that should have happened and did not. Line-by-line checking before acceptance is not distrust; it is how the Act was designed to be used. For you: In the RRR belt every landowner conversation reaches “what if the road takes it?” The developer who can sketch this formula on a napkin — deeds-based value × multiplier + solatium + structures + 12% clock — becomes the most credible person the family has met. And for the land bank: parcels NEAR an alignment appreciate; parcels ON it get the formula — which pays better where registration culture is honest. 2026-11-25|ls-gpa-risk: Power of attorney for property: why a GPA sale is risky Land School · source: “Power of Attorney for Property: Why a GPA Sale is Risky” by 1acre.in Key Highlights A PoA creates an AGENCY: someone may act on the owner’s behalf. It transfers no ownership, ever. Suraj Lamp v. State of Haryana (Supreme Court, 2011): only a registered sale deed conveys immovable property. A 2025 Supreme Court ruling repeated it: a GPA — even paired with an agreement to sell — does not create title. Genuine GPAs remain perfectly valid for MANAGEMENT — the classic case being NRIs and family members handling property from afar. A deal where the GPA is the transaction itself is a deal to pause and lawyer-check. What a power of attorney for property is One person — the principal — signs a document authorising another — the agent (attorney holder) — to act for them on a specific property: collect rent, pay dues, sign routine paperwork, represent them before authorities when they cannot be present. The land stays the principal’s throughout. Definition — Principal / agent: the owner giving the authority, and the person receiving it. Every power the agent has flows from the principal — and stops when the principal cancels it or dies. What a legitimate GPA typically covers A clean GPA spells out a limited, specific set of powers, never a vague catch-all. Read it for five things: scope — does it name the property, survey number, and the exact permitted actions? Sale authorisation — explicit words allowing price negotiation, deed execution and receiving payment (general “manage my affairs” language is NOT enough to sell); duration — open-ended, or tied to one period or transaction? Registration details — which SRO registered the GPA itself, and its number; revocation clause — how the principal can cancel it. When a GPA is genuinely needed Owners cannot attend every signature and filing. Legitimate uses cluster at three stages: pre-purchase — an NRI authorising a relative to negotiate while abroad; registration — an owner who cannot travel authorising someone to complete SRO formalities; post-purchase — ongoing management, rent, taxes, maintenance. The problem begins the moment a GPA is used INSTEAD of a sale deed — as a way to skip stamp duty and keep the deal off the record. Example: The old “GPA sale”: seller hands over a GPA + agreement to sell, buyer pays full price, both save duty, nothing registers as a transfer. Cheap and invisible — until an heir, a creditor or the seller himself reappears. Everything that made it cheap made it worthless. Red flags in GPA-based deals — severity and checks Issue Severity What to check No legal title transfer behind the deal High Confirm a registered sale deed exists or will be executed — never just a GPA Same GPA used for multiple sales High Search the SRO records for earlier transactions on the property GPA revoked without notice High Verify directly with the principal that it is still active Vague or expired authority Medium Read for explicit sale/price/execution powers and the validity period Principal dead or incapacitated High Confirm the principal’s current status before relying on the holder Unregistered / notarised-only GPA Medium Insist on a GPA registered at the SRO for anything consequential Power of attorney vs registered sale deed Aspect Power of attorney Registered sale deed Purpose Authorises someone to ACT for the owner Legally transfers ownership Where issued SRO (or notarised for limited non-transfer uses) SRO only Validity Until revoked, expired, or the principal dies Permanent, until a future lawful transfer Typical use Management, remote representation, execution help Actual sale, purchase or gift Cost Duty on the GPA itself — small, varies by state Full stamp duty + registration on the transaction value A GPA is right when someone must act for an owner. A registered deed is the ONLY right instrument when ownership itself must move. Treating the two as interchangeable is where most GPA disputes are born. Is a PoA reliable? Only as reliable as its registration and the principal’s continuing authority. The classic failures: relying on an old GPA nobody confirmed was unrevoked; accepting a notarised-only document where registration was required; assuming a GPA survives the principal’s death (it does not — agency ends at death, with a narrow exception where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property). After Suraj Lamp, several states issued circulars tightening registration practice — another reason to verify at the SRO rather than trust the paper shown. Definition — Agency coupled with interest: the narrow exception where the agent has a real stake in the property itself — such authority can survive revocation and death. It is the legitimate backbone of a builder’s PoA inside a registered JDA. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ GPA registered at the SRO — note the number. ☐ It explicitly authorises sale, price negotiation and deed execution. ☐ The principal personally confirms it is unrevoked (a video call is cheap). ☐ The principal was alive and competent when it was signed — and is alive now. ☐ The actual transfer happens by registered sale deed, with the principal as vendor. ☐ A property lawyer reads any deal where a GPA carries real weight. Quick answers (FAQ) Is a GPA sale legal in India? As a transfer of ownership — no. Since Suraj Lamp (2011), only a registered deed conveys property. Can a GPA holder sell on the owner’s behalf? Yes — IF the GPA expressly authorises sale, and the deed is registered naming the principal as seller. The holder signs FOR the owner; he never becomes the owner. What happens to a GPA when the principal dies? It dies too. Anything signed after is void — except the narrow coupled-with-interest case. Does a PoA transfer ownership? Never, however it is worded. How do I verify a GPA before a purchase? Registration at the SRO, express powers in the text, principal alive and confirming — the three checks that cover almost everything. Bottom line A power of attorney is a genuinely useful management tool that was never designed to replace a sale deed. Buyers who keep that line bright — and verify registration and current validity before relying on one — avoid nearly all the GPA grief that ends up in court. For you: In your JD work, PoAs are daily equipment — landowners grant you development authority, NRI owners send registration authority. Draft them task-scoped and registered; and when one appears on the OTHER side of the table, run the three checks before the price conversation. 2026-11-25|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School · source: “Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-11-27|ls-poa-rules: Power of Attorney for land: rules, risks, and what holds up in court Land School · source: “Power of Attorney for Land: Rules, Risks, and What Actually Holds Up in Court” by 1acre.in Key Highlights A PoA authorises someone to ACT for you — sign, register, manage, negotiate. It can never hand over ownership. Suraj Lamp (Supreme Court, 2011) settled it: a PoA is not a title-transfer instrument; Shakeel Ahmed (2023) confirmed old GPA chains get no pass. A PoA normally DIES with the principal (Section 201) — except where the agent holds a real interest in the property (Section 202). Registration is mandatory whenever a PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer. Stamp duty turns on the relationship: close family pay nominal rates; unrelated buyers/developers face conveyance-level charges. What a PoA actually does for land One person — the principal — authorises another — the agent — to act on their behalf: signing agreements, handling Sub-Registrar paperwork, managing tenants, negotiating a sale. Representative authority only. The persistent confusion is treating a PoA as a stand-in for a sale — it is not and cannot be: under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, only a REGISTERED SALE DEED transfers title to immovable property. GPA vs SPA: picking the instrument A General PoA grants sweeping authority — suited to an NRI overseeing property across years and distance, but broad authority is hard to police, and if the agent oversteps, the very breadth makes the overstep harder to prove. A Special PoA is built for ONE job and expires when it is done. For land, advocates lean SPA: narrow scope, less room for misuse, cleaner record. What the Supreme Court has said Suraj Lamp (2011) : the “GPA sale” — the once-common practice of selling property via GPA + agreement + will, skipping the sale deed and its stamp duty — transfers NO title. Shakeel Ahmed (2023) : confirmed the principle applies to old chains too — decades-old GPA transactions do not ripen into ownership with time. If your seller’s ownership story runs through a GPA instead of a registered deed, there is no ownership in the story. Example: A Shamshabad plot is offered cheap: the “owner” bought it in 2008 “on GPA” from the recorded owner and has possession ever since. Under Suraj Lamp he owns nothing — only the recorded owner (or their heirs) can convey. The fix, if everyone is alive and willing: a proper registered sale deed from the true owner now, with duty paid. Without that, the plot is unbuyable at any discount. The five classic PoA risks 1) Revoked but presented as valid — an unregistered cancellation shows no outward sign, so a revoked PoA can still deceive a third party. 2) Death of the principal — agency ends automatically under Section 201; anything signed after is void — except the narrow Section 202 case where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property itself. 3) Tangled chains of sub-authority — each PoA granting power to the next makes true ownership harder to trace; buyers inherit disputes they never saw. 4) Self-dealing — an agent selling to HIMSELF is valid only if the PoA explicitly permits it; otherwise a breach of fiduciary duty. 5) Missing registration — where a PoA permits sale, gift or transfer, registration at the sub-registrar is not optional; skipping it guts the document’s standing. Definition — Section 202 (Contract Act): the exception that makes a PoA survive the principal’s death: when the agent has a real INTEREST in the property (say, money already advanced against it), the authority is coupled with that interest and does not lapse. Everything else dies with the principal. Registration, stamp duty, validity Registration is mandatory when the PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer; a PoA limited to rent collection follows lighter rules. Stamp duty follows the relationship : close family typically nominal; an unrelated buyer or developer holding a sale-empowering PoA can face conveyance-level duty — precisely to kill the GPA-sale dodge. NRIs : execute before the Indian mission (or apostille in Hague-convention countries) and stamp within three months of the document reaching India. How to verify a land PoA before acting on it ☐ The PoA names the exact survey number, the exact act, and a duration. ☐ Registered, where the sale/irrevocable/interest test applies. ☐ A revocation clause built in from day one. ☐ The principal INDEPENDENTLY confirmed as owner — in the state land record, not the PoA’s own recitals. ☐ The principal confirmed ALIVE (for a Section 201 document, this is not a formality). ☐ EC pulled — showing any PoA, mortgage or transaction already registered against the parcel. ☐ The land itself transferable — no assigned/prohibited/acquisition taint, because no PoA overrides a land-law restriction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a PoA be used to SELL land? An agent under a valid, registered, sale-empowering PoA can EXECUTE a sale deed for the owner — but the PoA itself never makes anyone an owner. Does calling it “irrevocable” make it irrevocable? No — the label doesn’t; only a genuine Section 202 interest does. What if the principal dies? Authority ends; post-death signatures are void (Section 202 excepted). Stamp duty? Relationship-dependent — nominal for close family, conveyance-level for unrelated sale-empowered holders. Bottom line A PoA is a tool for ACTING at a distance, not for owning. Verify the principal, the registration, the scope and the land’s own transferability — and treat any ownership chain that runs through a GPA as a chain with a missing link. For you: Two rules for your desk. Buying: any parcel whose chain contains a “GPA sale” is unpriced risk — either the true owner signs a fresh registered deed or you pass. Structuring your own JDs: the development GPA you take from landowners should be SPECIAL, scoped to the project, registered, with the JDA’s reversion clause mirrored in it — broad GPAs frighten landowners and courts alike. Lis pendens binds a new buyer to a pending case’s outcome even if nobody told them it existed. Revenue-court disputes and old village claims are often NOT online — a physical visit still counts. What checking for disputes actually means There is a difference between a title that LOOKS fine and one that has been CHECKED. Land carries history the deed never shows: an old inheritance quarrel, a boundary shifted after a family split, a loan never cleared. A litigation check confirms — through independent sources, never the seller’s word — that none of this is unresolved. Two different searches get confused: the EC tracks registered financial claims; a court search tracks live litigation. A property can be clean on one and dirty on the other. What a proper check covers Encumbrance history — loans, mortgages, claims, from the SRO. Court cases — anything involving the owner or the property, via eCourts and the NJDG. Ownership and survey records — mutation entries cross-checked against the deed. Unrecorded local disputes — boundary and revenue matters not yet digital. The neighbours — who usually know about a fight before any court does. Why the check must happen before you pay anything Land fights make up a striking share of India’s pending civil cases, tracing to a few causes: contested inheritance, forged papers, unclear titles, encroachment. A seller with a pending case usually will not mention it. The check matters at three moments: before the offer, before any advance, and before registration — each later stage makes a discovered defect more expensive. Definition — Lis pendens: “suit pending”. Once litigation over land is on foot, whoever buys the land inherits the case’s outcome — knowledge or ignorance makes no difference. The law assumes you searched. Start with the Encumbrance Certificate Ask for at least 15 years, ideally 30 — a spotless five-year EC says nothing about a fifteen-year-old dispute that never resolved. Read it for court attachments, unreleased liens, and windows where entries abruptly stop; a gap is a question, not a quirk. Then search eCourts and the NJDG Both portals cover District and High Courts, searchable by party name, case number or type — free. Search the owner’s name in every reasonable variation (initials, spellings), the FAMILY’S names, and past owners’ names from the chain. A nil result under one spelling proves only that spelling. Example: A buyer near Shamshabad stopped at a clean EC. The seller’s sister’s partition suit was two minutes away on eCourts — under HER name. The court notice arrived after his registration; lis pendens did the rest. Red flags — what they usually mean, what to do Red flag What it usually means What to do EC entries suddenly stop A dispute or transaction may have been kept off the record Ask the SRO for a written explanation of the gap eCourts returns nothing at all The case may sit under a name variant Re-search with initials and past owners’ names Seller resists the full-period EC Possibly avoiding an older entry Insist on the 15–30 year window — non-negotiable Neighbours mention a fight the seller did not Local knowledge runs ahead of filings Visit the tahsildar; investigate before any advance Title changed hands fast and often Rapid resales can be laundering a defect Trace and check each prior owner in the chain The physical checks documents cannot replace Revenue-court records — at the tahsildar or sub-divisional office — are mostly not digitised; someone must go and look. Neighbours help more than expected. For anything beyond a small purchase, a lawyer running the full search is cheap against the alternative. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC for 15–30 years. ☐ eCourts + NJDG searched under every reasonable name variation. ☐ Ownership and survey details cross-checked on the state portal. ☐ SRO and revenue office visited for what is not online. ☐ Neighbours asked about disputes and boundaries. ☐ Lawyer’s full search before any advance. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I search property litigation online free? Yes — eCourts and NJDG. Do all disputes show there? No — revenue matters and fresh village fights often exist offline first. What if I unknowingly buy disputed land? Lis pendens binds you to the outcome; your recourse is against the seller — which is why the check precedes the money. How far back should the EC go? 30 years where possible; 15 as the floor. Bottom line Disputes rarely announce themselves; they sit in old entries and filings the seller has no reason to mention. A few hours across the EC, eCourts and one village visit cost almost nothing against untangling a case later. F9 · The third flop in three days — Thursday’s auction of eight HUDA Heights plots in Banjara Hills, covered in this paper’s Thursday and Friday editions, had already drawn zero bids before Friday’s two further failures. Mechanics: three HMDA land parcels — one ultra-prime (Banjara Hills), one politically contested (Moosapet) and one plain commercial repeat-offender (Neopolis Plot 17) — all failed inside a single week, which is the pattern this Deep Dive exists to unpack. F10 · Why bidders reportedly stayed away — outlets attribute the result to high upset prices — one report cites investors wanting closer to ₹80 crore per acre for Moosapet against its fixed ₹99 crore floor — compounded, for Moosapet specifically, by the ongoing BRS protest campaign around the land. Incentives: a serious bidder has to weigh not just the price but the reputational and legal-risk cost of being the buyer who “took truckers’ land” in a live political fight — a cost that does not show up on any balance sheet but shows up directly in who chooses not to bid. Plain English: this is a real gap in the public record, not an oversight in this paper’s research — the state’s entire legal defence rests on this replacement already existing, and no source independently confirms it does. The deeper force behind this week is the same cash-strapped land-monetisation push this paper flagged in Wednesday’s and Thursday’s editions — Telangana cabinet sub-committees pushing land auctions specifically to raise revenue, and the state separately carrying roughly ₹8 lakh crore in total debt including guarantees. What this week adds is a second, independent check on that push beyond the courts: the market itself. A government can win every legal argument over a parcel and still find that nobody wants to buy it at the price set, and that failure costs the exchequer real, immediate revenue regardless of how any court case ends. What a ten-year follower of Hyderabad land politics knows, that a first-time reader doesn’t: HMDA auctions run in large batches precisely so that a few headline successes (this paper has tracked Kokapet parcels fetching ₹115–151 crore per acre earlier in 2025–26) can coexist with, and visually offset, multiple quiet failures in the same window — a single top-line auction revenue figure for a notification period can mask exactly this kind of three-flops-in-a-week pattern underneath it. 🎯 So what — stakes and consequences The state loses, for now, the combined floor-price revenue of both Friday parcels — roughly ₹311.85 crore for Moosapet alone, with Neopolis Plot 17 worth considerably more again at its ₹120-crore-per-acre floor — and must now decide whether to cut prices, wait out the political heat, or both before re-auctioning. BRS loses nothing by losing the PILs: its political warning that these sales were unpopular and poorly priced looks, if anything, reinforced by what the market just did. Truckers and transport workers using the Moosapet yard get a practical reprieve, win or lose in court, simply because there is no buyer yet to displace them. Watch: (1) whether HMDA cuts the upset prices meaningfully for the promised January–February re-auction (likelihood: moderate-to-high, given officials are already reviewing “what went wrong”); (2) whether Harish Rao’s “future government will reclaim it” pledge turns into any concrete Assembly motion rather than a standalone statement (likelihood: low, consistent with the debate-challenge pattern in today’s separate Telangana Politics story); (3) whether either petitioner appeals Friday’s dismissal (likelihood: low, no source mentions one); (4) whether the alternative ORR-outside truck-parking sites are confirmed operational (likelihood: unclear — genuinely unknown from available sources). What this means for you: (a) for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate — a court clearing a sale is necessary but nowhere near sufficient for that sale to actually happen at the price asked; before Vivek ever treats a government auction’s upset price as a market benchmark, he should check whether that exact auction actually cleared, not just whether it was legally allowed to proceed. (b) for business and investing generally — political controversy is a price-suppressing factor that exists independently of legal risk, and a disciplined buyer prices it as its own separate line item rather than folding it into generic “title risk.” The beginner mistake: assuming “the court cleared it” means the asset is now straightforwardly desirable. The sharper, expert read: a court-cleared, title-clean government auction that still draws zero bids is the loudest, cheapest, most public price signal available — and it just happened twice, on two unrelated plots, in the same afternoon. ⭐ The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map The Telangana High Court dismissed both PILs against HMDA’s sale of the disputed Moosapet truck-park land on Friday, clearing every legal obstacle to the auction. The auction still drew zero bids — and so did a completely unrelated Kokapet Neopolis plot auctioned the same day, the third HMDA parcel to fail in a single week after Thursday’s eight-plot Banjara Hills flop. HMDA is now reviewing its pricing and plans a January–February re-auction; BRS, having lost in court, keeps the political fight alive on its own separate track. The lesson sits exactly at the gap between the two outcomes: legally clear and commercially wanted are different questions, and this week answered them differently on the very same parcels. 2026-11-28|ls-plot-safe: How to check if a plot is legally safe to buy Land School · source: “How to Check If a Plot Is Legally Safe to Buy in India” by 1acre.in Key Highlights With plots, nobody upstream has checked anything — legal verification is entirely your job. The 30-year title chain proves a seller CAN sell; the latest deed alone proves little. An EC only catches REGISTERED transactions — deposit-of-deeds mortgages and court cases need separate searches. ULPIN, the 14-digit parcel ID, catches an altered survey number. The whole drill costs a few thousand rupees; a disputed title costs years. Why verification matters MORE for plots Buy a flat and a builder, a lender and usually a RERA registration have each done a slice of checking before you arrived. Buy a plot and NONE of that happened. Vacant land also carries a messier past — split among siblings after a death, handed around inside a family, converted from farmland years ago with paperwork that never caught up. Every one of those moments is a place a defect could have entered the record and stayed. Verification is finding them BEFORE you pay. Start with the title chain, not the latest deed A sale deed tells you who holds the land — nothing about whether the person BEFORE them had any right to hand it over, and that gap is where most disputes begin. Ask for the Mother Deed, then trace every sale, gift, partition and inheritance forward. Thirty years is the working standard — your bank will stop at a 13-year EC, but that is a LENDING threshold, not a title standard. Inheritance deserves special attention: in ancestral property every coparcener holds a share and ALL must sign; a guardian selling a minor’s share needs court permission; one absent signature can unwind a sale a decade later. The EC catches less than you think Owning land and being FREE to sell it are separate things. Pull the EC yourself from the sub-registrar for the full 30 years — in most southern states a clean result returns as Form 16, while Form 15 lists whatever is registered against the property. Now the part sellers rarely volunteer: the EC shows only REGISTERED transactions. A mortgage created by depositing title deeds with a bank often never reaches the register; neither will an unregistered sale agreement, an oral family partition, or unpaid dues. So run two more searches: the e-courts portal for litigation on the survey number, and the state land-records portal for the latest revenue record — comparing owner name, survey number, extent and classification against the deed. Any mismatch: investigate before proceeding. Definition — Equitable mortgage (deposit of title deeds): a loan secured by simply handing the original deeds to the bank — legally valid, and frequently invisible on the EC. It is why “show me the ORIGINALS” is a due-diligence question, not rudeness: a seller without originals may have a banker holding them. Zoning, conversion and RERA: what you can actually build Start with the master plan — how is the parcel classified? Farmland once? Ask for the conversion ORDER and the fee receipt; a seller’s assurance is not a document. Then RERA: larger plotted developments generally must register, and an unregistered one becomes a problem YOU inherit. Then who may buy at all — agricultural-land eligibility varies by state. And layout approval sits with the planning authority — verified separately, on its portal, by its LP number. Legal checks vs physical checks Check What it proves Where you get it 30-year title chain The seller’s right to sell Sub-registrar copies + your advocate EC (30 years) Registered loans/claims Sub-registrar / online e-courts search Pending litigation ecourts portal, by survey number/parties Revenue record State’s view of owner + classification State land-records portal (Dharani in TG) Licensed survey Ground matches paper Surveyor on site ULPIN check Parcel identity not altered State records where rolled out Walk the boundary before you pay A licensed surveyor measures the plot against the deed AND the revenue record — paper and ground drift apart more often than buyers expect. Where your state has rolled it out, check ULPIN — the 14-digit parcel ID under the national land-records programme, sometimes called Bhu-Aadhaar — which nails the parcel’s identity against an altered or misquoted survey number. Warning signs of a risky purchase Survey numbers that DISAGREE across deed, revenue record and EC. A PoA sale where the PoA is unregistered or does not explicitly authorise sale. A seller who produces photocopies every time and originals never. Land on a prohibited-property list — the Sub-Registrar will refuse it until the restriction resolves. And resistance to a NEWSPAPER NOTICE: publishing one inviting objections before closing is ordinary practice — a seller who argues against it is telling you something. Example: The newspaper notice is the cheapest trap-detector in the kit: ₹3,000, one column, fifteen days. A silent fortnight closes the deal with confidence; a phone call from an unknown “co-owner” just saved you the whole purchase price. Quick answers (FAQ) How far back should the chain go? 30 years. Does the EC show every loan? No — registered ones only; deposit-of-deeds mortgages hide. Do all plots need RERA? Larger plotted developments generally yes; small ones may be exempt — check the threshold. Is patta proof of ownership? Supporting evidence only. Do I need a lawyer for a small plot? Yes — defect risk does not scale down with plot size; a small plot with a bad title is 100% bad. Bottom line Chain, EC, courts, record, zoning, survey — six checks, each catching what the others miss, none substituting for the rest. A few thousand rupees of verification against years of litigation: the cheapest insurance in real estate. For you: This lesson is the customer’s-eye view of everything your school has covered — use it as your master checklist template. Better: run the six checks on your OWN ventures and publish the results as a buyer pack. In a market where verification is “entirely the buyer’s job”, the developer who does the job FOR the buyer owns the trust premium.
